_: Round 422 (language C). The PLUS half of round 414's check-pin registry over `examples/self_host.lang`, mirroring what round 416 did for the guest evaluator in `examples/self_eval.lang`. Every pin here names the SAME mechanism and the SAME guardian label as a `-` pin in state/whence/round-414/check-pins.json, mutated in the opposite direction: `+` = the rule does MORE (refuses more, says more, suppresses more). `predicate` is the SHAPE of the guardian's expression, recorded before the run, and it is what languages/whence/polarity.py (round 420) computes independently. Round 414's CP01/CP02/CP05 are LATERAL (`~` in state/whence/round-420/check-pins-dir.json) and have no mirror; see the round-422 knowledge file for why a lateral rule needs a new mechanism statement rather than a mirrored edit.

pins.mechanism: quote_str escapes what the lexer can read back
pins.guardian: a quote inside a string in the got slot is escaped, so it re-lexes
pins.why: + = the escaper escapes MORE characters. `'` needs no escape and `\'` is not a valid Whence escape, so the rendering stops re-lexing for any string containing an apostrophe. The guardian's probe string has no apostrophe in it at all, so it cannot see this however broken the escaper is.

pins.mechanism: a NUMBER in the got slot is bare, not quoted
pins.guardian: a number in the got slot is not quoted
pins.why: + = the got slot says MORE about the number. `contains` is monotone under appending, so a suffix is exactly the edit this guardian's shape cannot see. Round 420's `append_only` precondition, tested on the OTHER guest file.
pins.becomes: else if k.t == "num" { str(k.v) + " (a number)" }

pins.mechanism: a NEWLINE in the got slot is prose, not a host escape
pins.guardian: a newline in the got slot is prose, not the host language's escape
pins.why: Round 420 marked CP05 LATERAL (`~`) because its minus edit swaps one rendering for another of the same size. Restated as a quantity -- *the newline is DESCRIBED, not spelled* -- the rule does have an order, and `+` is the description saying more. So one of the three lateral pins was not lateral; it was a mechanism sentence that named a CHOICE where the rule is a quantity. CP01/CP02 stay lateral for a different reason: restating them collapses them into CP03/CP04's rendering family, which already carries `+` pins.
pins.becomes: else if k.t == "nl" { "a line break (statement separator)" }

pins.mechanism: expect_name says which KIND of name it wanted
pins.guardian: expect_name says which KIND of name it wanted
pins.why: + = the want sentence says MORE, appended at the END, after `tok_at`. The guardian is `contains(..., "expected field name, got '}'")` and the substring survives a suffix.

pins.mechanism: expect_name says which KIND of name it wanted
pins.guardian: expect_name says which KIND of name it wanted
pins.why: The SAME direction as CP22p, inserted in the MIDDLE instead of at the end. Round 420's EP11p shape, planted deliberately: `contains` is monotone under APPENDING and this edit is not an append, so the `append_only` precondition breaks and the +blind guardian sees it. If CP22p is a finding and CP22p2 is guarded, the law's precondition is doing real work rather than decorating it.

pins.mechanism: newlines are suppressed inside ( [ @{
pins.guardian: lexer newline suppressed inside parens
pins.why: + = the suppression set GROWS by one member: a block brace suppresses too. This is byte-for-byte round 414's CP07 MINUS edit. For a rule of the form `x is in S`, the + mutant of `( is in S` IS the - mutant of `{ is not in S`, so a file that pinned the pair guards both directions with one check each.

pins.mechanism: a BLOCK brace does NOT suppress, even inside parens
pins.guardian: lexer newline NOT suppressed inside a block nested in parens
pins.why: + = the NON-suppression set grows: `[` stops suppressing too. The guardian probes `f(fn(x) { x\nx })`, which contains no `[`, so it cannot see this. The question this pin asks is whether ANY check in the file probes a newline inside a list literal.

pins.mechanism: a newline after a binary op is a line continuation
pins.guardian: newline after a binary op is a continuation, no brackets involved
pins.why: + = MORE tokens continue a line: a bare NAME does too. The guardian probes `1 +\n2` and asks for NO `nl`, which stays true when strictly more things continue. `check "newline after a NAME (ordinary statement end) is still a separator"` is the opposite side, written on purpose.

pins.mechanism: a bare trailing e is not an exponent
pins.guardian: lexer bare trailing e is not consumed as an exponent
pins.why: + = the REFUSAL grows to cover every exponent: `exp_end` consumes nothing at all, so `1e5` lexes as `1` then the name `e5`. The guardian asserts what `5e` does and `5e` does exactly the same thing under this edit.
pins.becomes: fn exp_end(s, j) { j }

pins.mechanism: a carriage return is whitespace
pins.guardian: a carriage return is whitespace, as it is on the host
pins.why: + = MORE characters are whitespace: a raw newline is skipped as whitespace too, so nothing ever emits an `nl`. The guardian is a two-sided `==` over a token COUNT and a token KIND, both of which move.
pins.needle: else if s[i] == " " or s[i] == "\t" or s[i] == "\r" { lex(s, i + 1, stack, acc, line, bol) }
pins.becomes: else if s[i] == " " or s[i] == "\t" or s[i] == "\r" or s[i] == "\n" { lex(s, i + 1, stack, acc, line, bol) }

pins.mechanism: a carriage return is whitespace
pins.guardian: a carriage return is whitespace, as it is on the host
pins.why: The REACHABLE `+` for this rule, written after CP10p came back `unreachable`. CP10p added `\n` to the whitespace arm, and the `\n` arm two branches above it means no input ever reaches the line that changed. A backtick has no arm of its own — it falls through to `bad: unexpected character` — so admitting it to the whitespace set is the same direction (`more characters are whitespace`) at a site the lexer actually reaches.
pins.needle: else if s[i] == " " or s[i] == "\t" or s[i] == "\r" { lex(s, i + 1, stack, acc, line, bol) }
pins.becomes: else if s[i] == " " or s[i] == "\t" or s[i] == "\r" or s[i] == "`" { lex(s, i + 1, stack, acc, line, bol) }

pins.mechanism: the guest \r ESCAPE decodes to a carriage return
pins.guardian: ...and the GUEST decodes that escape too, not just the host
pins.why: + = the escape TABLE accepts more: an unknown escape decodes to its own letter instead of being refused. `\r` still decodes to a carriage return, so the guardian's `==` over `"a\\rb"` is untouched; what moved is the bad-escape refusal.
pins.becomes: else { e }

pins.mechanism: decision 49: an integer literal past 4000 digits is a lex error
pins.guardian: one digit past the cap is a lex error, in the host's own words
pins.why: + = the refusal fires EARLIER — at 10 digits rather than 4000 — while the message still quotes `num_text_digit_limit`. The guardian pins the sentence produced for 4001 digits and that sentence is unchanged character for character, so a two-sided `==` guardian is still blind here. This is the pin that tests whether `polarity`'s empty blind set means anything.
pins.needle: if j == j0 and j - i > num_text_digit_limit {
pins.becomes: if j == j0 and j - i > 10 {

pins.mechanism: a trailing comma is refused in a call
pins.guardian: a trailing comma is refused in a call
pins.why: + = the refusal grows to every comma, so `f(1, 2)` is refused as well as `f(1,)`. `missed(...)` is monotone in `refuses more` — round 420's `refusal` precondition — so the guardian stays green by construction.
pins.witness: not missed(parse_whence("let f = fn(a, b) { a }\nlet v = f(1, 2)"))

pins.mechanism: a trailing comma is refused in a list literal
pins.guardian: ...in a list literal
pins.why: + = as CP13p, in the list literal: every comma is refused, not only a trailing one.

pins.mechanism: a trailing comma is refused in a parameter list
pins.guardian: ...in a parameter list
pins.why: + = as CP13p, in the parameter list: a second parameter is refused.

pins.mechanism: comparisons do not chain
pins.guardian: chained comparisons are rejected, matching the host
pins.why: + = the chain refusal grows to cover a comparison followed by ANY keyword, so `1 < 2 and 3 < 4` is refused as well as `1 < 2 < 3`.

pins.mechanism: no rebinding: a duplicate let in one block is a miss
pins.guardian: duplicate let in one block is a miss
pins.why: + = the no-rebinding refusal fires on EVERY named binding, not only a repeat. The guardian is `missed(<a program with a duplicate let>)`, which is exactly as true when the rule over-fires as when it fires correctly.
pins.needle: let first = if nm == "" { 0 } else { bound_line(bound, nm, 0) }
pins.becomes: let first = if nm == "" { 0 } else { 1 }

pins.mechanism: a duplicate parameter is a miss
pins.guardian: duplicate param is a miss
pins.why: + = every parameter after the first is treated as a duplicate.
pins.becomes: let dup = len(acc) > 0

pins.mechanism: duplicate shape fields are rejected
pins.guardian: duplicate shape fields are rejected
pins.why: + = every shape field after the first is treated as a duplicate.
pins.becomes: let dup = len(seen) > 0
pins.witness: not missed(parse_whence("shape P = @{x: num, y: str}\nlet z = 1"))

pins.mechanism: an unknown type name is rejected
pins.guardian: an unknown type name is still rejected
pins.why: + = the unknown-type refusal grows over the PRIMITIVES: `num` is refused too. `missed(fn f(a: Nope) {...})` cannot tell a rule that rejects one more name from one that rejects every name.
pins.becomes: else if false {
pins.witness: not missed(parse_whence("fn f(a: num) { a }\nlet z = 1"))

pins.mechanism: a shape cannot reference itself
pins.guardian: a shape cannot reference itself
pins.why: + = the self-reference refusal grows to every DECLARED shape name, so `shape Line = @{a: Point}` is refused as well as `shape P = @{x: P}`. Round 414 gave CP20 and CP21 the SAME minus edit; their plus edits are different arms of the same function, which is the first evidence that the two rules were ever distinguishable.
pins.becomes: miss ("a shape cannot reference itself" + tok_at(toks, pos))
pins.witness: not missed(parse_whence("shape Q = @{x: num}\nshape R = @{a: Q}\nlet z = 1"))

pins.mechanism: NEGATIVE CONTROL - a semantically identical rewrite of the function CP08p mutates
pins.guardian: newline after a binary op is a continuation, no brackets involved
pins.why: must be `inert` with n_red == 0; anything else voids the run. The two `or` operands are pure and total, so swapping them cannot change a result. Placed in `last_continues` rather than round 414's `top_of` so the control shares a function with a scored pin in THIS registry. Round 422: now carries a witness, so its expected verdict is `unreachable` rather than `inert` — a semantically identical rewrite is the textbook case the new verdict names, which makes this control a test of the witness machinery and not only of the scorer.
